title: Interfaith families
hook: some Jews live in interfaith families, and communities respond in different ways

segments.voice: Yesterday, cultural Jews, and the line culture counts. Did you pass a recipe, a word or a song on to someone? Today, families where two traditions share one table. Day one thousand forty-nine.

A couple sits at a kitchen table with a notebook, planning a wedding. One of them is Jewish. The other isn't. The guest list is easy. The menu is easy. Then come the questions nobody wants to say out loud. Who will marry us? Under a chuppah, or not? And later, quietly: if we have children, what will they be? Their two families are listening from a distance, hoping, worrying, loving them both. Jewish communities have been asked this question for a long time, and they don't all give the same answer.
screen: `A NOTEBOOK AND A WEDDING.` → `WHO WILL MARRY US?` → `WHAT WILL THE CHILDREN BE?`

segments.voice: Begin with the Torah, because it holds more than one view. Moses marries Zipporah, the daughter of Jethro, a priest of Midian. Later, Jethro visits and watches Moses judging the people from morning until evening, alone, worn down. He tells his son-in-law to share the load, and the text says: "So Moses hearkened to the voice of his father-in-law, and did all that he had said." The great lawgiver takes advice from a priest of another people. But the same Torah also warns against marrying into the nations of Canaan, for fear the children will be turned away from God. And in the book of Ezra, returning exiles are told to send away foreign wives. The Bible doesn't settle this in one verse. The rabbis then made a rule about children: in the Mishnah, a child's Jewish status follows the mother. That rule still shapes communities today, and they respond in different ways. Orthodox communities hold to traditional Jewish law: their rabbis don't officiate at interfaith weddings, and the child of a Jewish mother is Jewish. Conservative communities also follow the mother's line, and some reach out warmly to interfaith families who come through the door. Reform and Reconstructionist communities in North America accept a child with one Jewish parent, mother or father, who is raised as a Jew, and some of their rabbis officiate at interfaith weddings while others don't. Each holds its position for reasons it cares about: continuity, law, welcome, love. Meanwhile, real families live it. A non-Jewish parent drives the kids to Hebrew school every week. Grandparents learn new holidays. A child carries two sets of stories. Today's line is honest, and short: families are complex.
screen: `MOSES LISTENS TO JETHRO.` · `THE TORAH ALSO WARNS.` · `STATUS THROUGH THE MOTHER, OR EITHER PARENT.` · `REAL FAMILIES LIVE IT.` · then, large: `FAMILIES ARE COMPLEX.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: welcome one family. Settle, and breathe slowly. Bring to mind a family you know that holds more than one tradition. It might be your own. It might be a neighbor's, or a friend's. Picture their table on a holiday. Who feels at home there, and who might feel a little on the edge? Now choose one small welcome you could offer. An invitation. A question asked with real interest: how do you celebrate? Learning the name of one of their holidays. If you pray, you can hold that family in prayer in your own words. If you don't, simply wish them well, one by one. The bell holds the time.
Interfaith families. Households where Jewish and other traditions share one table, met by Jewish communities in different ways. Today's word.
Your line: families are complex. Today, when you hear about someone's family, hold back the quick verdict. Ask one more question, and listen. Day one thousand forty-nine.

howItsDone: Jewish communities respond to interfaith families in different ways: Orthodox and Conservative communities follow descent through the mother and their rabbis generally do not officiate at interfaith weddings, while Reform and Reconstructionist communities accept a child of either Jewish parent raised as a Jew, and some of their rabbis officiate.

fork.setup: you're Moses, judging the people alone from morning until evening. your father-in-law, a priest of Midian, says you'll wear yourself out. what do you do?
options: thank him, and keep doing it all yourself.
listen to him, and share the load as he says.
step down, and let someone else lead.
fork.reveal: Moses listens, and does all that Jethro said. the great lawgiver takes advice from a priest of another people.

original.note: Hebrew: family. In the Bible it can mean a whole clan.

trapdoor: what you thought: Judaism has one fixed answer about interfaith families.
what it means: communities respond differently, from traditional law to open welcome, and families live in the middle of it.
what a scholar hears: the Bible holds both Jethro's advice and Ezra's demand, and the Mishnah traces a child's status through the mother.

notes: Claims rule: index hook says 'many Jews live in interfaith families'; hook field softened to 'some Jews'. No intermarriage statistics or dates (e.g., the Reform resolution year) are given.
